doc.title: 68088_Wilbur B. Ware, Sr oral history interview

chapter: Return to New York in the late 1960s
title: Elvin Jones at Pookie's Pub and pianist Billy Greene
summary: Ware subs for Wilbur Little in Elvin Jones' group and tells a story of Billy Greene's name on the sign.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: After that, I went into Minton's with Blue Mitchell and [unintelligible] that, I went down to see Elvin Jones. I hadn't seen him since I'd been back in New York. He was working down on Hudson Street in a little place called Pookie's Pub (PHONETIC). It was across the street from the Half Note. The Half Note is kind of famous. This is on, say, like Monday night. Blue worked the weekends.

They had Duke Drew Pearson (PHONETIC), big band over there on Monday nights or either Clark Terry and his big band on Monday night. On weekends, Elvin and Joe Farrell (PHONETIC) and little Billy Greene (PHONETIC) was on piano, my hometown friend, and that's where I was hooked up with Whitney Balliett (PHONETIC) from New Yorker Magazine. He come in. He always would write something about me, I noticed, through the years, you know. I was surprised to see him. But he'd come down there to write about Elvin -- well, Elvin and Wilbur Little -- Wilbur Little was playing bass when I went down there. When I walked in, Wilbur say, "I'm glad to see you. I've got to go off on the road for a month and if you want to, I'm sure Elvin give you the key until I come back." Elvin say, "Sure." Well, this was a gig for me, you know?

I made that. But I've got to tell you this. Billy Greene was a little pianist. He's short in stature and he's kind of -- it seems like he's got it in for anybody taller than him. Good piano player, good musician. But he's never received any kind of recognition from anybody. He was very vocal about that. It comes to mind, one night --
He's on Elvin, (inaudible) Heavy Sounds album.
That's right. He and Richard Davis and Hal Mabern. Al made one. Billy wrote one of the tunes on that, you know.
Right. inaudible, I think it was.

Yeah, something like that. Well, anyway, he stated that -- he tells me out in front of the club one night. "See, got your names out here." This is just a little bar, you know, just a small bandstand -- we just can get up there on the bandstand -- and Billy says, "Why won't you let me put my name out here?" I said, "Man, why are you worrying about that?" I said, "We know you're in there." He said, "Okay."
Well, Billy got a piece of tape, put his name on it and stuck it on there.
The next night we come to work, he says, "See that, Wilbur? They even tore that off there." He was funny, a beautiful cat.
